title: Plans and farewells
goal: Talking about plans, hopes and the future — then closing twenty units with a conversation that uses almost everything you've learned.
bekal: talk about plans, intentions and hopes for the future
use *гэж бодож байна* for "I'm thinking of"
say goodbye warmly and keep the connection alive

dialogs.title: Яриа — Дараагийн жил
dialogs.intro: Budi's semester is almost over. He and Sarnai sit in a tea house, talking about what comes next.

notes: ⚠️ **… гэж бодож байна = "I'm thinking of …"** — the most common pattern for a plan that isn't fixed yet. *Дахин ирнэ **гэж бодож байна*** = I'm thinking of coming again. Notice that *гэж* closes off the content of the thought, just like quotation marks.

**Mongolian has no separate future form** — the *-на* form covers "will" as well as "now". What marks the future is the time word: *маргааш*, *ирэх жил*, *хоёр жилийн дараа*. **Much like English "I'm leaving tomorrow"**, where the time word does the work.

**Унуулна from унах + -уул: "make ride", i.e. take someone riding.** The *-уул / -үүл* suffix turns a verb into "make or have someone do it" — like English "make someone ride" packed into one word. You'll meet this suffix everywhere at A2.

**Чамаар бахархаж байна = "I'm proud of you".** Notice the *-аар* suffix you know from unit 10, used here for the cause of the pride. Many feelings in Mongolian pair with a particular suffix, so learn them together with their suffix.

**Дараа уулзтал баяртай literally means "be joyful until we meet again".** The *-тал / -тэл* suffix means "until". It's a warm, open-ended goodbye — the way Mongolians part from people they hope will return.

grammars.title: Talking about the future
body: Five patterns cover everything you need, and none of them needs a new verb form. What sets them apart is **how certain** the plan is.
after: ⚠️ **Байх at the end of a sentence is one of the most typical words in Mongolian and is used constantly.** It softens a statement into a guess: *Хол байх* (it's probably far), *Ирэх байх* (he'll probably come). It's like English "I guess" or "probably" — and using it makes you sound like a native speaker, not a textbook.

**Future time words to master:** *маргааш* (tomorrow), *нөгөөдөр* (the day after tomorrow), *ирэх долоо хоногт* (next week), *ирэх сард* (next month), *ирэх жил* (next year), *хоёр жилийн дараа* (in two years), *удахгүй* (soon), *хожим* (someday).

grammars.title: Everything you've mastered, in one table
body: These are twenty units boiled down to fifteen rows. Read it once, then close the book and try to make one sentence for each row about your own life.

head: What you can do
The tools
Unit
rows: Tell the time and make plans

after: If you can make a sentence for ten of those fifteen rows without turning to another page, **you've truly reached A1** — not just the A1 printed on the cover.
What you don't have yet is speed, and speed doesn't come from books. It comes from halting, mistake-filled, repeated conversations. This book has done its part.

English

blocks.title: Asking about other people's plans
items: *Дараа нь юу хийх вэ?* — What are you doing after this?
*Ирэх жил юу хийх вэ?* — What are you doing next year?
*Хэзээ буцах вэ?* — When are you going back?
*Дахин ирэх үү?* — Will you come again?

head: Монгол
Say it
When to use it
rows: Until we meet again. The warmest.
Have a good journey, for long trips.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Get the pair *сайн яваарай* and *сайн сууж байгаарай* right, because they're used every day and mixing them up sounds funny straight away. The one **staying** says "go well"; the one **leaving** says "stay well". English has a hint of this in "take care" versus "see you, I'm off".

blocks.title: Keeping the connection alive
items: *Долоо хоногт нэг удаа ярилцъя.* — Let's talk once a week.
*Видеогоор залгая.* — Let's do a video call.
*Монголд ирвэл заавал хэлээрэй.* — If you come to Mongolia, you must let me know.

sections.title: What's waiting for you at A2

blocks.text: You now have about three hundred active words, seven cases in the singular, present and past verbs, vowel harmony that's starting to run on its own, and Mongolian Cyrillic you can read without spelling it out. What comes next isn't harder — it's what makes your sentences **longer and smoother**.

head: What comes next
Example
Why it's useful
rows: "At my own friend's house" — three suffixes in one word.
"A person who reads a lot" — a whole sentence becomes an adjective.
"Is read" — unlocks half of written Mongolian.
"Make someone read" — one root, four meanings.
"Turned out he came" — the signature sound of every folk tale.

blocks.title: The three most useful things to do this week
items: **Reread every dialog from Unit 1 onward, in order, over two days.** Unit 1 will feel almost ridiculously easy — proof that the book works.
**Write five sentences a day about your own day.** *Өнөөдөр би гэртээ ажилласан. Оройдоо мах идсэн.* The mistakes that show up there are your real mistakes.
**Find someone to talk to before you feel ready.** Mongolians almost never meet foreigners who speak their language; their patience with beginners is nearly endless.
I'm thinking of going to the Gobi.
